title: Direct Volume Access
summary: Direct volume access means opening a raw handle to a whole logical volume rather than to a file inside it, so a program reads and writes the underlying file system structures itself. Because the read does not travel through the normal file path, file level permissions, access checks and the file system filter drivers that record file activity may never see the operation. Attackers use it to copy registry hives, locked database files or the contents of an entire drive, and they often reach for built-in utilities such as vssadmin, wbadmin or esentutl to build a shadow copy and then pull data out of that copy. The artefacts are indirect: a volume device handle opened by an unusual process, shadow copy creation, related service or driver loads, and command lines captured in Windows Security event 4688 or Sysmon event 1. Backup agents, forensic imaging tools and some endpoint scanners open volume handles legitimately, so the defender compares the parent process, the account, the timing, and whether the volume was only read or actually altered.

beginner.definition: Direct volume access means a program opens a whole disk or disk partition, not a single file on it. The program then reads the file system records itself. This can let it copy files that are locked or protected. The normal permission checks on individual files may be skipped altogether.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many important files are locked while the computer runs, such as the registry and the event logs. A backup program reads them by opening the volume directly instead. An attacker can use the same trick to copy those files and study them later. Security tools that watch files may see nothing, because no file was opened in the usual way.
howItWorks: The program opens the raw volume path for a disk, not a path to a file.
It reads the file system structure to find where each file starts and how long it is.
It copies bytes straight from the disk, so a lock on one file does not stop it.
It may ask a backup service to make a shadow copy, then read from that copy instead.
It writes the copied data to another disk or sends it over the network.
Careful attackers delete the tool and the copy, leaving only a few system records behind.
beginner.example: Imagine a library where every book is chained to its shelf. To borrow one, you ask the librarian, who checks your membership card and writes the request in a log book. Direct volume access is like driving a forklift through the loading bay at night. You lift the whole shelf and take it away. The front desk never handled a request, so nothing was written down. The books were never unlocked, but they left the building with you.
takeaways: A program can read a disk without opening a single file, so file level logs may stay empty.
Shadow copy tools have honest uses, so judge them by who ran them and what happened next.
Watch for volume handles, backup utility use and sudden large copies on servers.

objectives: Explain how opening a raw volume differs from opening a normal file, and why that matters.
Describe the artefacts that direct volume access leaves in process and service telemetry.
Distinguish legitimate backup or imaging activity from attacker staging with the same tools.
Identify which kinds of data an attacker targets with direct reads of a volume.
Outline detection ideas such as unusual volume handles and unexpected shadow copy creation.
